The Battle of Wagram. On July 5 and 6, 1809, Napoleon achieved a hard-fought victory over the Austrian army under Archduke Charles near Vienna during the War of the Fifth Coalition. Approximately 177,000 French troops and German allies faced 145,000 Austrian forces. Though less decisive than many Napoleonic victories and achieved only after a full two-day battle of maneuver and attrition, it demonstrated that Austrian military reforms had made them a formidable opponent. The battle was a close contest. The Austrian army under Archduke Charles fought well and nearly broke the French center multiple times through disciplined counterattacks. Both days saw intense fighting across the Marchfeld plain. The French gradually wore down the Austrians through superior coordination and reserves, finally breaking their right flank on the second day. Austrian casualties were approximately 40,000. French losses were approximately 34,000, a much closer engagement than Napoleon's previous victories. Austria signed the Treaty of Schönbrunn, ceding Salzburg, parts of Poland, and Galicia to France and its allies, and paying a large indemnity. Unlike after other defeats, Austria retained enough strength and territory to remain a great power. Within a few years, it would join the Coalition against Napoleon. The battle demonstrated that Archduke Charles had successfully reformed and modernized the Austrian army, making it a genuine threat to French dominance.
